g.text: Tensor operations: einops, broadcasting, indexing, einsum. Foundations for every later exercise.
A tensor is a multi-dim array with SHAPE (tuple of ints) and NAMED ROLES for each dim.
Every operation is 'reshape + reduce'. Einops makes the shape/role explicit.
of shapes. Einops makes it named.
arr[b, c, h, w] → flat index:
Instead of .view()/.permute() with numeric dims, use STRINGS with NAMES.
Same operation, but the intent is legible.
Common patterns (all equivalent to raw torch operations)
rearrange(arr, 'b c h w -> b c w h')
rearrange(arr, 'b c h w -> b c (h w)')
rearrange(arr, 'b c h w -> (b h) c w')
rearrange(arr, 'b c (h1 h2) w -> b c h1 h2 w', h2=2)
einops.rearrange(arr, 'b c h w -> b h (c w)') # intent obvious
Each dim gets a NAME (letter or word). Format: <input pattern> -> <output pattern>
• Same name in both sides = same axis, possibly reordered.
• (a b) means 'a * b elements in that dim'. Splits: pass factor as kwarg. Merges: just write (a b).
Wrong pattern → clear error at parse time (not silent tensor mishap).
reduce: collapse dims with mean/max/sum. repeat: expand dims.
(h w) grouping is the killer feature: pool, unroll, split all in one line.
reduce(arr, 'b c h w -> b c', 'sum')
reduce(arr, 'b c (h1 2) (w1 2) -> b c h1 w1', 'max')
Expand: introduce new dims by copying
repeat(x, 'c h w -> 3 c h w')
The (h1 h2) grouping trick - the killer feature
One idea: split a dim of size h into TWO named factors (h1, h2) where h = h1*h2
Then rearrange or reduce over h1, h2 independently.
reduce(x, 'b c (h1 2) (w1 2) -> b c h1 w1', 'max')
rearrange(x, 'b s (h d) -> b s h d', h=n_heads)
When two tensors have DIFFERENT shapes, PyTorch tries to make them compatible.
Rules: align RIGHT, then each dim must MATCH or be 1.
align right; A has 2 dims, B has 1
B is virtually repeated along dim 0
Given tensors A (shape s_A) and B (shape s_B), pad the shorter with 1s on the LEFT.
• A.dim == 1 and B.dim > 1 → broadcast A along this dim
• A.dim > 1 and B.dim == 1 → broadcast B along this dim
Result shape: max of the two along each dim.
unsqueeze / squeeze: add/remove size-1 dims to align.
arr.unsqueeze(0) # (H, W) → (1, H, W) # so shape aligns with (B, H, W)
Silent bug: (3, 4) + (3,) FAILS. You wanted the (3,) to be per-row broadcast, but rules align RIGHT.

einsum: multiply + sum in one line
Any tensor operation involving product-and-sum can be written as einsum.
Matmul, batched matmul, attention, and every linear algebra op are einsum patterns.
Anatomy of a single einsum call
einsum(A, B, 'i j, j k -> i k')
In A and in output → this axis is KEPT (row axis of A)
In A and B but NOT in output → this axis is SUMMED
In B and in output → this axis is KEPT (col axis of B)
out[i, k] = sum_j A[i, j] * B[j, k]
'b i j, b j k -> b i k'
'b s h d, b t h d -> b h s t'
Q dot K.T per head, per batch
'b h s t, b t h d -> b s h d'
attn weights dot V per head, per batch
1. Same letter in multiple inputs = tensors must have same size along that axis.
2. Letter in inputs but NOT in output = SUM OVER that axis.
3. Letter in output but NOT in inputs = ERROR (nothing to broadcast).
4. Letter appearing 3+ times = repeated multiplication (elementwise per index).
Under the hood: broadcast to align → elementwise multiply → sum over missing letters. That's it.
Indexing, gather, argmax: picking specific elements
Different way to think: not 'reshape' but 'pick these values'.
gather is the most under-taught operation and shows up everywhere.
arr.gather(dim, index) where arr.shape == index.shape (except along `dim`)
For every position (i, j, k, ..) in index:
→ output shape = index shape. Along `dim`, output picks whatever `index` says.
The unifying ideas that reappear everywhere.
